paragraphs: In a bandit problem, a learner repeatedly chooses interventions and observes their outcomes, trying to avoid losing too much reward while learning which intervention is best. Additional observed variables can improve this process when they form a d-separator between intervention and outcome. The practical difficulty is that a learner may not know whether those variables satisfy the required causal condition.

This paper formalizes adaptivity to that uncertainty. The desired behavior is to approach the performance of a method that already knows whether a d-separator is available. The proposed algorithm uses the observed variables without requiring that advance knowledge, addressing the risk of relying on a causal relationship that does not actually hold.

When a d-separator is observed, the algorithm achieves optimal regret and improves on classical minimax methods. When the variables are not a d-separator, it incurs substantially less regret than recent causal bandit algorithms. The paper also extends its adaptivity framework to conditions including the front-door criterion, broadening the kinds of causal information it can accommodate.
neurips-2022-adaptively-exploiting-d-sep.tldr: An adaptive causal bandit algorithm benefits from observed d-separators without needing advance knowledge that they are present.

paragraphs: Spatio-temporal sequences contain relationships across both locations and time. A model must decide how to combine those relationships: it can process spatial structure first, temporal structure first, or both together. The paper argues that committing to one manually designed ordering can make it difficult to match the dependencies that matter for different tasks.

The authors introduce UniST, a unified attention-based architecture that supports all three priorities. Its S2T module handles space before time, T2S handles time before space, and STS treats the two dimensions synchronously. Building these options into one framework makes the choice of modeling priority flexible rather than requiring separate architectures for each approach.

AutoST adds a network architecture search strategy that automatically searches for the modeling priority within UniST. Across five real-world datasets, the authors report state-of-the-art performance even when UniST uses only one of the three module types, with further strong performance from AutoST. These findings support adapting the organization of spatial and temporal processing to the task.
neurips-2022-autost-towards-the-universa.tldr: AutoST searches how a unified attention architecture should prioritize spatial and temporal relationships for a given task.

paragraphs: Efficient coding offers a way to connect what a neural network computes with how its activity evolves. In spiking networks, the idea is to represent low-dimensional stimulus signals efficiently by minimizing a time-dependent loss associated with coding information through spikes. To explain biological circuits, however, such models also need to respect properties of real neurons and their connections.

This paper revisits efficient coding to construct a more biologically plausible generalized leaky integrate-and-fire network. The model includes excitatory and inhibitory neurons, fast and slow synaptic currents, and local currents associated with adaptation and rebound. It also allows neurons to differ in their firing thresholds, resets, and postsynaptic potentials, alongside structured connectivity of low rank.

The contribution is a model that realizes efficient coding while incorporating this richer collection of biological features. The authors also show how the rank of connections among excitatory neurons shapes network responses. This links a specific structural property of the network to its dynamics within an efficient-coding account.
neurips-2022-biologically-plausible-solu.tldr: The paper builds efficient-coding spiking networks with richer biological features and connects excitatory connectivity rank to network responses.

paragraphs: Shortcut learning occurs when a network uses easy predictive features without learning the semantic structure that a task is meant to require. Generative models might seem protected because they aim to represent data more comprehensively. This paper shows that generative modeling alone is insufficient to prevent shortcuts, challenging that proposed source of protection.

The authors instead exploit an observation about how shortcuts are represented: they tend to be encoded using little information. Chroma-VAE first trains a variational autoencoder classifier to concentrate the shortcut in a small part of its latent representation. It then trains a second classifier on the complementary latent subspace, which is intended to exclude the shortcut information.

This two-stage design makes the organization of the representation central to reducing shortcut reliance. The authors demonstrate its effectiveness on benchmark and real-world shortcut-learning tasks. Their findings also suggest a broader possibility: deliberately manipulating a generative classifier's latent space may help isolate or interpret particular correlations, rather than merely accepting whatever representation ordinary training produces.
neurips-2022-chroma-vae-mitigating-short.tldr: Chroma-VAE mitigates shortcut learning by isolating shortcut information in a small latent subspace and classifying from the remaining representation.

paragraphs: CLIP learns image representations using natural-language supervision and can transfer to new tasks without task-specific training. This paper identifies an explaining-away problem in which it focuses on a few features while overlooking other relevant ones. The authors attribute this behavior to insufficient extraction of covariance structure: information about which features occur together in the multimodal data.

CLOOB addresses that problem with modern Hopfield networks, which retrieve embeddings enriched by feature co-occurrences in stored embeddings. However, this enrichment increases a saturation effect in CLIP's InfoNCE training objective, hampering learning. The method therefore pairs Hopfield retrieval with the InfoLOOB objective, which is introduced to reduce that saturation.

The two components serve complementary purposes: one enriches the representation, while the other supports learning with that enrichment. After pretraining on Conceptual Captions and YFCC, the authors compare zero-shot transfer against CLIP on other datasets. CLOOB performs better across all architectures and datasets considered in those experiments, supporting the combined design within the evaluated settings.
neurips-2022-cloob-modern-hopfield-netwo.tldr: CLOOB combines Hopfield-based feature enrichment with InfoLOOB training and outperforms CLIP in the reported zero-shot transfer comparisons.

paragraphs: Langevin algorithms combine gradient-based updates with added noise and are used for sampling, optimization, and learning. Their analysis asks how close the algorithm's distribution gets to a target distribution after a finite number of steps. Constraints and non-convex losses complicate that question, making convergence guarantees especially useful for understanding these methods.

The paper studies non-convex losses under polyhedral constraints, which need not define a bounded region. It also allows data variables satisfying an L-mixing condition, extending the analysis beyond independent and identically distributed data. Distance to the target is measured using 1-Wasserstein distance, giving a common basis for comparing the stated convergence bounds.

The authors obtain a deviation bound of O(T^(-1/2) log T). The previous constrained result described in the abstract was O(T^(-1/4) (log T)^(1/2)) for a compact convex domain with independent data. The new result improves the stated constrained bound and matches the best-known unconstrained bound, while applying to the paper's specified dependence and constraint conditions.
neurips-2022-constrained-langevin-algori.tldr: The paper establishes an improved finite-time Langevin convergence bound for non-convex losses with L-mixing data and potentially unbounded polyhedral constraints.

paragraphs: Graph-based recommenders use connections between users and items to capture relationships extending beyond direct interactions. However, highly active users and popular items can introduce popularity bias, while noisy interactions can distort the learned representation. Contrastive approaches address these issues by creating multiple graph views and encouraging their representations to agree.

The paper questions two parts of that process. Random or rule-based removal of nodes and edges may produce unsuitable views, and maximizing agreement can preserve information unrelated to recommendation. Its CGI framework learns which edges or nodes to remove as part of end-to-end training, making the graph structure itself an adaptive component.

CGI also introduces an information bottleneck into contrastive learning to discourage the capture of irrelevant information shared across views. Together, the components aim to improve both the views being compared and the information retained from their comparison. Experiments on public datasets show significant improvements over strong baselines, supporting this combination for the recommendation settings studied.
neurips-2022-contrastive-graph-structure.tldr: CGI jointly learns graph augmentations and filters irrelevant shared information to improve graph-based recommendation.

paragraphs: Compositional data describe relative parts of a whole and lie on a simplex, making their structure different from ordinary unconstrained numerical features. Such data arise in microbiome analysis, geochemistry, and other applications. This paper develops augmentation methods for that setting, extending an approach widely used in vision and language to a different kind of input.

The proposed transformations draw on compositional data analysis, particularly Aitchison geometry and subcompositions. These principles guide augmentation around the structure of compositional observations. The authors incorporate the resulting methods into standard supervised learning pipelines, making augmentation the intervention rather than requiring an entirely new predictive pipeline.

Across a broad collection of benchmark datasets, the augmentations produce consistent performance gains. The authors report new state-of-the-art results for disease prediction tasks involving colorectal cancer, type 2 diabetes, and Crohn's disease. They also use the augmentations to build a contrastive learning model that improves on previous microbiome representation-learning approaches, showing benefits for both supervised prediction and learned representations.
neurips-2022-data-augmentation-for-compo.tldr: Augmentations designed for compositional data improve microbiome prediction and support a stronger contrastive representation-learning model.

paragraphs: Meta learning uses experience across tasks, so its generalization analysis must account for both shared knowledge and task-specific learning. Information-theoretic analysis and classical learning theory have offered different ways to study this problem. The paper takes a step toward connecting them through generalization bounds based on evaluated conditional mutual information, or e-CMI.

To demonstrate what the framework can express, the authors consider tasks whose predictors combine a shared representation h with a task-specific function f_i. With n samples from each of N tasks, their bound scales as the square root of C(H)/(nN) + C(F)/n, where the two complexity terms describe the shared representation class and task-specific function class.

The structure of this bound distinguishes the two learning burdens. The shared-representation term benefits from samples across tasks, while the task-specific term depends on the samples within a task. This scaling matches a previously reported Gaussian-complexity result for the setting, showing that the e-CMI framework can recover a meaningful classical guarantee for meta learning.
neurips-2022-evaluated-cmi-bounds-for-me.tldr: New e-CMI generalization bounds recover classical complexity scaling for meta learning with shared representations and task-specific predictors.

paragraphs: Model attributions help explain neural-network predictions, but imperceptible input changes can disrupt those explanations. A key measure of attribution protection is Kendall's rank correlation, which tracks agreement between rankings. Because that measure is not differentiable, it is difficult to use directly as an objective for training a more stable explanation mechanism.

The paper shows that expected Kendall's rank correlation is positively correlated with cosine similarity. This motivates focusing on the direction of attribution vectors. The authors use that perspective to analyze shortcomings of defenses based on l_p norms and propose an integrated gradient regularizer, or IGR, that maximizes cosine similarity between attributions for natural and perturbed inputs.

Their analysis also connects IGR to encouraging neurons to retain the same activation states across an input and its perturbed counterpart. Experiments across different models and datasets support the attribution-protection analysis and show an improvement in adversarial robustness. The work therefore links a ranking-based explanation criterion to a directional training objective and to changes in internal network behavior.
neurips-2022-exploiting-the-relationship.tldr: IGR protects model attributions by aligning their directions across natural and perturbed inputs, motivated by a link to rank correlation.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning under a fixed sampling budget when each action selects a set of arms and returns feedback for every selected arm. The aim is to identify optimal arms before the budget runs out. Unlike simpler formulations, an arm's feedback may depend on which other arms were selected alongside it.

The setting is also non-stochastic: feedback may be generated by an oblivious adversary rather than by a fixed random reward distribution. The authors build a theoretical framework covering both numerical feedback and preference-based feedback, while ensuring that meaningful notions of optimal arms can still be defined under these broader conditions.

They propose a generic algorithm encompassing elimination strategies ranging from aggressive removal of candidates to more conservative decisions. The analysis establishes sufficient and necessary sampling budgets for the algorithm to find the best arm and derives lower bounds applying to any learning algorithm in this setting. These results clarify how the available budget constrains identification when feedback depends on the selected group.
neurips-2022-finding-optimal-arms-in-non.tldr: The paper develops an arm-elimination framework and budget guarantees for non-stochastic combinatorial bandits with subset-dependent feedback.

paragraphs: Algorithmic alignment is the idea that a neural network can learn a reasoning task more efficiently when its components match the structure of the target algorithm. Graph neural networks are often described as aligned with dynamic programming, a strategy that builds solutions from related subproblems. This paper asks how broadly and rigorously that connection can be established.

Using category theory and abstract algebra, the authors expose a connection between graph neural networks and dynamic programming that extends beyond observations about individual algorithms such as Bellman-Ford. The contribution gives a mathematical basis for reasoning about the relationship, rather than relying only on similarities noticed in particular examples.

The authors use this connection to verify several earlier findings and to design more theoretically grounded graph neural networks for tasks centered on edges. They also present empirical results on the CLRS algorithmic reasoning benchmark. The work offers a foundation for architecture design guided by algorithm structure, with the stated aim of enabling stronger algorithmically aligned networks.
neurips-2022-graph-neural-networks-are-d.tldr: The paper develops an algebraic connection between graph neural networks and dynamic programming and uses it to guide architectures for edge-centric tasks.

paragraphs: In fully decentralized cooperative reinforcement learning, agents cannot access global information such as the actions of other agents. Independent Q-learning is a natural option, but each agent learns while the others change their policies. Consequently, the transition probabilities it experiences keep changing, and convergence of ordinary independent Q-learning is not guaranteed.

The paper introduces stationary ideal transition probabilities under which independent Q-learning could converge to the global optimum. I2Q then models this ideal transition function and performs independent Q-learning on it. Crucially, that modeling is fully decentralized and independent of the policies learned by other agents, addressing the source of non-stationarity identified by the authors.

The proposed route to optimal learning therefore rests on the modeled ideal transitions rather than directly treating the changing interaction process as stationary. Empirically, I2Q achieves substantial improvements across a variety of cooperative multi-agent tasks. These results support the approach of changing the transition model used for learning while preserving the decentralized information setting.
neurips-2022-i2q-a-fully-decentralized-q.tldr: I2Q models stationary ideal transitions to address non-stationarity in fully decentralized cooperative Q-learning.

paragraphs: Finding an object in a 3D scene from a verbal description often requires understanding its position relative to other objects. Recognizing that several objects are chairs is insufficient when the description distinguishes one by its location or proximity to a window. The paper targets this relational part of matching language to objects in point-cloud scenes.

The authors propose a language-conditioned transformer with spatial self-attention that accounts for relative distances and orientations between objects. Joint training with visual and language inputs teaches the model to use those spatial relationships when resolving a description. A teacher-student approach further supports learning: the teacher first uses ground-truth object labels, then helps train a student that operates on point-cloud inputs.

Ablation studies show advantages of the proposed approach, and the complete model significantly outperforms the stated prior state of the art on Nr3D, Sr3D, and ScanRefer. The results support explicitly representing spatial relations and using label-informed teaching to improve language-guided object localization.
neurips-2022-language-conditioned-spatia.tldr: A language-conditioned transformer uses spatial relations and teacher-student training to improve object localization in 3D scenes.

paragraphs: Multiple views can help distinguish objects that look similar from a single angle. Existing datasets can make this problem less representative of real use by relying on synthetic or coarse categories, omitting validation splits, or lacking annotations about how informative individual views are. MVP-N is introduced to support closer study of real-world, fine-grained multi-view classification.

The dataset contains 44 retail products, around 16,000 captured views, and 9,000 multi-view sets. Its view-level annotations record human-perceived information quantity, enabling analysis of how much a view contributes. Because different product classes can look alike from particular angles, the dataset also naturally includes multi-view label noise associated with that visual similarity.

The authors benchmark four methods for aggregating features across views and twelve soft-label methods. This combination supports studying both how to combine observations and how to learn when individual views are ambiguous. The reported experiments position MVP-N as a resource for developing multi-view classification methods under these real-world conditions.
neurips-2022-mvp-n-a-dataset-and-benchma.tldr: MVP-N provides real multi-view retail-product images, view informativeness annotations, and benchmarks for classification with naturally ambiguous views.

paragraphs: In this bandit setting, an action's expected payoff can increase the longer it has gone unused. Choosing an action therefore affects both the reward available now and its opportunity to recharge. This captures behavior relevant to recommendations and advertising, but it creates a difficult scheduling problem: optimal planning is NP-hard even when the payoff functions are already known.

For known payoff functions, the paper combines randomized rounding of a linear program with an interleaved scheduling method that coordinates choices over time. The resulting polynomial-time algorithm achieves a 1 − 1/e approximation asymptotically and in expectation. This improves on the previous 1/4 guarantee for the setting allowing at most one action per round.

The algorithm also improves prior guarantees when several actions can be selected in each round. Finally, the authors transform the planner into a bandit algorithm for initially unknown payoff functions, obtaining sublinear regret. That extension connects better scheduling with learning the recharging behavior from experience, while retaining the stated theoretical performance guarantees.
neurips-2022-non-stationary-bandits-unde.tldr: A randomized scheduling method improves approximation guarantees for recharging-payoff bandits and extends to unknown payoffs with sublinear regret.

paragraphs: Deep clustering uses neural networks to group data without supervised class labels and has become especially effective for high-dimensional images. This paper examines whether that success also comes with resistance to adversarial manipulation. It addresses a gap in the principled study of attacks and robustness for deep clustering, beyond earlier work on traditional clustering methods.

The authors propose a black-box attack based on a generative adversarial network. The attacker does not know which deep clustering model is operating but can submit queries and observe its outputs. Evaluations across multiple state-of-the-art models and real-world datasets find the attack highly successful, showing vulnerability under this limited-access setting.

The study also tests natural unsupervised defenses, which fail to mitigate the proposed attack in the reported evaluations. An attack on the production Face++ face-clustering API substantially reduces its performance as well. Together, these findings motivate stronger robustness methods for deep clustering and show that the concern extends to an evaluated deployed service.
neurips-2022-on-the-robustness-of-deep-c.tldr: A GAN-based black-box attack exposes vulnerabilities in deep clustering models and Face++, while the tested unsupervised defenses fail to mitigate it.

paragraphs: Acceleration frameworks aim to reduce the work needed to solve optimization problems, but the steps they require can themselves be costly. This paper modifies Monteiro-Svaiter acceleration to remove an expensive implicit equation that otherwise must be solved at every iteration. The change directly targets overhead within the acceleration procedure.

For convex optimization with a Lipschitz pth derivative, for any p of at least two, the variant improves complexity by a logarithmic factor and matches a lower bound. The authors also introduce an adaptive subproblem solver that needs no knowledge of problem parameters. It can be implemented as a second-order method using linear-system solves or as a first-order method using MinRes.

The practical comparisons are mixed in an informative way. On logistic regression problems, the method outperforms previous accelerated second-order methods but falls behind Newton's method. Simply repeating the adaptive first-order subproblem solver is competitive with L-BFGS. Thus, the paper combines an optimal theoretical complexity result with empirical evidence that depends on which competing method is considered.
neurips-2022-optimal-and-adaptive-montei.tldr: A revised Monteiro-Svaiter framework removes costly implicit solves, matches a convex-optimization lower bound, and introduces a parameter-adaptive subproblem solver.

paragraphs: Bayes-adaptive Markov decision processes formalize how an agent should balance gathering information with earning rewards. Exact Bayesian reinforcement-learning solutions are computationally intractable, so practical work often turns to approximations. This paper first asks what makes planning difficult, focusing on the effort required to resolve uncertainty about the environment.

Under mild structural assumptions, the authors define a planning complexity measure that captures the worst-case difficulty of acquiring information and exhausting epistemic uncertainty. They illustrate its significance with an exact planning algorithm that uses the measure to obtain more efficient planning. The algorithm nevertheless remains computationally intractable, so this step establishes the measure's relevance without providing a practical exact solution.

The paper then introduces a particular state abstraction intended to reduce the complexity of the Bayesian planning problem. This abstraction gives rise to a computationally tractable approximate planner. The overall contribution connects the difficulty of learning about an environment to planning design, with abstraction offering a potential way to reduce that difficulty.
neurips-2022-planning-to-the-information.tldr: The paper measures Bayesian planning difficulty through information acquisition and develops an epistemic state abstraction for tractable approximate planning.

paragraphs: Source-code summarization generates a short description of what a code snippet does. The paper starts from the observation that programmers understand code at several levels, including statements, tokens, and subtokens. These levels emphasize different information: statements help express overall logic, while smaller textual pieces contribute meaning through names and other fine-grained details.

The proposed method transforms code into a pyramidal representation that includes these different granularities and their relationships. A pyramid attention mechanism then aggregates features efficiently across the hierarchy. The resulting transformer, PA-former, is designed to bring coarse logical information and fine textual information into the same summarization process.

On two source-code summarization benchmarks, PA-former surpasses previous methods and achieves the reported state-of-the-art results. The findings support the usefulness of organizing code representations around multiple conceptual levels. Rather than relying on just one level of description, the architecture explicitly makes relationships among levels available when learning to generate a concise functional summary.
neurips-2022-pyramid-attention-for-sourc.tldr: PA-former summarizes code using pyramid attention to combine statement-, token-, and subtoken-level information.

paragraphs: Object detectors deployed in open environments need to recognize when an object falls outside the distribution they were trained to handle. Distance-based approaches have shown promise for whole-image classification, but their use at the object level has been less explored. SIREN develops such an approach using a representation space that can support different detector architectures.

The framework first shapes object representations through a trainable loss. It organizes them as a mixture of von Mises-Fisher distributions on a unit hypersphere, giving the learned representation a specific directional structure. At test time, an out-of-distribution score uses these learned distributions through either a parametric or a non-parametric approach.

This couples representation learning with the subsequent detection rule: the training stage creates the structure that the test-time score uses. The authors report competitive results for both detection transformers and CNN-based models, with a large AUROC improvement over the previous best method. Those evaluations support the framework's applicability across the two tested architecture families.
neurips-2022-siren-shaping-representatio.tldr: SIREN shapes object representations into directional distributions and uses that structure to detect out-of-distribution objects across detector architectures.

paragraphs: Continual learning must absorb new tasks while retaining performance on earlier ones. Much of its research targets this forgetting problem, but repeated training can also be too expensive for resource-limited devices. SparCL addresses both concerns by introducing sparsity throughout the continual-learning process, aiming to reduce computation while preserving accuracy.

The framework combines three mechanisms. Task-aware dynamic masking maintains a sparse network, dynamic data removal excludes less informative training examples, and dynamic gradient masking makes parameter updates sparse. The authors report that each mechanism contributes to efficiency and also helps mitigate catastrophic forgetting, making their combination relevant to both cost and retention.

Applied to existing state-of-the-art continual-learning methods, SparCL consistently improves training efficiency, with reported reductions in training FLOPs reaching a factor of 23 and accuracy gains reaching 1.7%. It also exceeds adapted sparse-training baselines in efficiency and accuracy. Evaluation on a real mobile phone further supports the practical potential of using this approach for continual learning on edge devices.
neurips-2022-sparcl-sparse-continual-lea.tldr: SparCL combines sparse weights, selective training data, and sparse gradients to reduce continual-learning cost while improving retention and accuracy.

paragraphs: Learning cooperative behavior usually depends on carefully designed rewards, which become harder to specify when several agents must coordinate. Unsupervised reinforcement learning offers an alternative, but encouraging a single agent to reach distinct states does not fully capture relationships among agents. SPD instead aims to learn varied coordination policies without extrinsic rewards.

The method represents relationships among agents at each time step using a Synergy Pattern Graph. It then measures how coordination patterns differ across episodes. Because an episode-level signal can be sparse, SPD decomposes this discrepancy into pseudo-rewards at individual time steps, providing more frequent learning signals for developing diverse forms of cooperation.

Experiments show meaningful behaviors, including maintaining formations in Multi-Agent Particle Environment and passing and shooting in Google Research Football. The authors also reuse the same pretrained policy parameters to initialize policies for multiple downstream tasks. In the reported football experiments, this improves data efficiency and outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, supporting coordination-focused pretraining as a useful starting point.
neurips-2022-spd-synergy-pattern-diversi.tldr: SPD learns diverse multi-agent coordination without extrinsic rewards and provides useful policy initializations for downstream cooperative tasks.

paragraphs: Agents trained from images often overfit to the appearance of their training environment. Image augmentation can increase visual diversity, but reinforcement learning adds a complication: a spatial change to an observation may alter its relationship to the recorded action or reward. Transformations useful in ordinary vision tasks therefore need additional care in this setting.

The paper proposes two guiding requirements: augmentations should encourage policies robust to distribution shifts and preserve compatibility with learning signals such as actions and rewards. Spectrum Random Masking approaches augmentation in the frequency domain. It is designed to encourage learning across the observation's full frequency spectrum while remaining compatible with the action and reward attached to the original observation.

Experiments on the DMControl Generalization Benchmark show state-of-the-art performance and strong generalization potential. These results support frequency-based augmentation as a way to increase useful visual variation for policy learning. The central contribution is connecting the augmentation design to both visual robustness and the meaning of the reinforcement-learning signals.
neurips-2022-spectrum-random-masking-for.tldr: Spectrum Random Masking augments observations in the frequency domain to improve visual reinforcement-learning generalization while preserving action and reward compatibility.

paragraphs: Compressing neural-network activations can reduce their resource demands, but image-to-image tasks are sensitive to aggressive quantization. Using fewer than four bits can work well for classification yet seriously degrade tasks such as semantic segmentation and depth estimation. This paper targets high-resolution activation maps with a compression method designed around that difficulty.

Wavelet Compressed Convolution, or WCC, applies an efficient, hardware-friendly Haar-wavelet transform and performs convolution on the compressed activation map. The method integrates compression with point-wise convolutions, which the abstract identifies as a major computational cost in modern architectures. Compression therefore becomes part of the convolutional operation itself.

Across experiments on tasks benefiting from high-resolution inputs, WCC combined with light quantization reaches compression rates equivalent to one- to four-bit activation quantization. The reported performance degradation is relatively small and more gradual. These findings support wavelet-based activation compression as a useful way to obtain substantial compression while better preserving performance on the evaluated image-to-image tasks.
neurips-2022-wavelet-feature-maps-compre.tldr: WCC combines Haar-wavelet activation compression with point-wise convolutions to achieve strong compression with gentler image-to-image performance degradation.
